english.html: vain superstitions and other such useless things. <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>

The said du Tilh, heard upon this bewitchment and sorcery, the names of the priests, and the ceremonies observed, answers in everything like the said de Rols, without failing in anything, adding, or diminishing. Proceeding to the confrontations, this du Tilh requires that the said de Rols be placed in sequestration and at liberty, to avoid subornation; which is ordered and executed.

We have shown above that the sequestration of goods, and still more of persons, is odious and prohibited, unless it be for some great and legitimate cause, such as is in this case the fear of seduction and subornation. <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>

notes.citation: Digest 43.30.3.4 (De liberis exhibendis, item ducendis, l. 3, within § 4 Iulianus ait, at the words Si vero utraque persona suspecta est; the print's sign before ſi verò is read as §); Decretals, X 2.13 (De restitutione spoliatorum), c. 8 Ex transmissa (printed ex tranmiſſa) and c. 13 Litteras; Decretals, X 2.19.14 (De probationibus, penultimate chapter, Causam matrimonii)
notes.original: l. iij. §. ſi ve rò vtraque. D. de lib. exhib. c. ex tran miſſa. c. literas de reſtit. ſpol. c. penul. de probã.

english.html: The confrontations completed, and objections [reproches] delivered by the said du Tilh, and a petition that he be permitted to publish a monitory letter [monitoire: letters read from the pulpit, calling on all who know anything to reveal it on pain of excommunication] upon the articles thereto attached concerning the pretended subornation of the said de Rols, by order he is admitted to verify the objections by him deduced; and nevertheless, considering the matter in question, to have the said monitory letter published, the better to know the truth; and it is ordered that inquiry shall be made on the court's own motion, as well in the places of Le Pin, Sagias and Artigat as in others neighbouring and necessary, as much upon the

At 12x: a small loop opening left at the top, a straight top bar, two bowls stacked on the right, and a tail running down-left below the foot. Read as the paragraph sign § (both readers; the citation is l. iij. § ſi verò vtraque, D. de liberis exhibendis = Dig. 43.30), the tail being what a capital B lacks; but the straight top bar reads like an italic swash B, and the corpus otherwise spells the sign out as 'parag.', so the sort may be a B. the line-end mark after 'ex' is a short stroke set at x-height (margin-2.jpg, x~540, y~770; seen at 10x normalized). Read as the word-break sign for 'ex|hib', transcribed as a single '-' per §1. It is the only such mark at the right edge of this note that sits on a line whose word is broken.

readings.reason: At 6x the numeral after 'l.' has three stems (i, i, j with descender) and three dots above: iij. The over-inked sign after it is kept as § (both readers): at 12x it shows a small loop opening left at the top, two bowls to the right and a tail running down and to the left below the foot; a capital B has a flat base and no tail. Its straight top bar is B-like, so escalated.
